cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, with a cross-nimbus, hangs on the cross between two angels, blood flowing from his wounds into a chalice below; a lion and a unicorn leap at the cross, soldiers at the left, one with a spear, divide his garments, and below figures cast lots. The image combines several verses: 'they pierced my hands and my feet … they part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture … save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns'.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-porta.summary: Around the entrance to the chapel, two concentric arcs of medallions frame the doorway: in the outer ring the bust of Christ at the top is flanked by the apostles, and in the inner ring the Virgin and Child are flanked by female saints. An antique window and an ancient urn sit above the door. The portal announces, before one enters, the heavenly company that fills the chapel within.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.

cur:monumental-sma-anastasis.summary: On a damaged wall, the figure of Christ in pale robes strides forcefully to the left, trampling the dark, prostrate figure of Hades beneath his feet as he reaches down to raise Adam. Though much of the painting is lost, the energy of the striding figure is still clear. It is among the earliest surviving images of the Anastasis anywhere.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.
Pope John VII (705–707) used Santa Maria Antiqua as his seat and had much of the church redecorated; most of the surviving paintings date from his time.

cur:objects-berlin-washing-of-feet-ivory.summary: Christ bends low over a basin to wash the feet of Peter, who sits at the head of the gathered apostles and raises his hand in protest. The other disciples crowd behind on a bench, watching, beneath a draped canopy; a Greek inscription names the scene. The image captures the humility of the Lord who 'came not to be served but to serve', a key moment in the Byzantine Passion cycle.
facts: In Byzantine art the Washing of the Feet is shown with Peter touching his head or raising his hand, recalling his words 'Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head' (iconographic tradition).
Small ivory icons of single feasts like this one were produced in Constantinople in the 10th century for private devotion (type).

cur:objects-gulbenkian-crucifixion-dipty.summary: Under an arched canopy Christ hangs on the cross, his head bowed and his body in a gentle curve, between the grieving Virgin and St John. Busts of angels appear in the upper corners and a small mound marks Golgotha at the foot of the cross. The warm tone of the ivory and the deep cutting give the figures a strong, almost sculptural presence.
facts: Leaves of this kind were once hinged to a companion panel, often showing the Virgin or another feast, to form a small folding icon (type).

cur:objects-gosforth-cross-crucifixion.summary: Near the foot of the east face of this slender Viking-age cross a small panel shows Christ crucified, arms outstretched, with a figure piercing his side with a lance and a woman with a long trailing dress below. The rest of the cross is covered with scenes from Norse mythology — the binding of Loki, the fight of Víðarr with the wolf — which the carver seems to have set in dialogue with the Christian story. Christ's death appears as the true victory over the powers of chaos.
facts: Wikipedia explains that the Crucifixion panel has been compared with the death of Baldr in Norse myth, the lance-bearer Longinus and Mary Magdalene paralleling figures of the pagan story, as a way of presenting Christianity to a Scandinavian audience.
The Victoria and Albert Museum had a cast of the cross made in 1882, shortly after its pagan imagery was recognised.
cur:objects-gosforth-cross-crucifixion.notes: Image is an 1883 engraving of the panel (public domain), not a photograph of the whole cross.
